name: Diego Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly lectures Monday to Wednesday, then labs on Thursday where we write Java until the room smells of cold coffee. I share a flat with three others near the tram line, and on Saturdays I work at a bike shop on Garrick Street. Money's okay because my mum helps with rent, but only part of it, so the bike shop wage covers my food and the rest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you choose software engineering?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I liked taking things apart as a kid, and a computer felt like the next thing to take apart. My mum is a nurse and my dad drives a delivery van, so a degree that leads to a steady desk job felt like the sensible move. I got in with ordinary grades, no scholarship, so I'm a bit nervous about whether I belong. And honestly, I don't use any of those AI chat tools. I don't trust them and I'd rather understand my own code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly that would be a relief. I'd say to my flatmates that the companies hyped it to raise money, and now everyone can calm down. Online I'd probably say nothing, because I stay off those arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still worry a bit. My course fees are covered by a loan, and the debt is real whatever AI does. But if the job market stays as it is, a degree like mine should still get me something decent in four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as now. Keep the Saturday shift at the bike shop, go to every lab, and start putting twenty pounds a month aside from the wage. I'd also join the university computing society, which my flatmate keeps nagging me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, I suppose. A bit boring, but boring is good when you're the first in your family at university. I still carry the loan worry, so it's not completely calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most in that quiet version of the world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan and rent, nothing to do with AI. My mum works double shifts to help me, and I feel guilty every time she sends money. If a bad year came, say the bike shop cut my hours, I'd be short fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what gets cut first if money tightens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going out with the flat, easily. Then I'd drop the gym and cook rice and beans in bulk. I would never tell my mum I'm struggling, though, which is probably a mistake.

say: I'd tell my flatmates the **hype** was always overdone and life carries on.
Online I'd stay quiet, because I avoid shouting matches about technology.
think: I'm still worried about the student **loan**, whatever AI does or doesn't do.
A computing degree should still lead to a decent job in four years.
do: Keep working Saturdays at the bike shop and **save** twenty pounds a month.
Join the university computing society this term and go to every lab.
feel: I feel **steady** but a little guilty about how much my mum sacrifices for me.
S0.quote: My mum works double shifts to help me, and I feel guilty every time she sends money.
fieldNote: Calm tone, but the worry is **money**, not AI; the loan and his mother's shifts sit under every answer.
He would hide a bad month from his mother, which is a real risk.
Avoids AI tools on principle, so even a quiet world leaves him slightly behind classmates.

steps.text: Keep the Saturday shift at the bike shop on Garrick Street
Put twenty pounds a month into a savings account
Skip nights out and cook rice and beans in bulk if money tightens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what happens when firms put profit before people. Online I'd back the union calls for rules on how companies use AI. At the bike shop I'd just joke that the robots can't fix a flat yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it scares me, because coding is exactly the thing they say AI takes first. Junior programmers are the ones who get hired for simple jobs, and those simple jobs are what a computer can do. I'm worried my degree is aimed at the exact target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course but I'd start asking lecturers which parts of software still need a human, like testing with real users or talking to clients. I'd still not touch the chat tools, but maybe I'd have to try one, just to know what I'm up against. I'd also ask if the university has a placement scheme, so I get a name on my CV early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. Honestly, this feels like someone moved the finish line after I started running. I was proud to get on this course and now I wonder if I picked the wrong one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools. Does that change if the whole industry does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the contradiction, yes. I'd hate it, but if every junior job asks for it I'd have to learn it, probably slowly and grumpily. I'd rather the government made firms train people than leave students to figure it out alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if graduates can't find work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies who keep the profits. And governments who let them. Not the students, and not really the technology, which is just a tool somebody decided to cut costs with.

say: I'd say firms are using AI to cut **costs** and we need rules and union voices.
At the bike shop I'd joke that robots can't fix a flat yet.
think: Coding is the exact work AI takes first, so my **degree** may be aimed at the target.
Junior programmer jobs are the ones I'm most afraid will shrink.
do: Ask lecturers which parts of software still need **people**, like testing and talking to clients.
Look for a placement scheme and try one AI tool, grumpily, to know the competition.
feel: It feels like the **finish line** moved after I started running, and I'm tense.
S1.quote: Honestly, this feels like someone moved the finish line after I started running.
fieldNote: Blames **companies** and governments, not the technology; consistent with his union-friendly outlook.
Admits he may have to use AI tools after refusing them, which he plainly dislikes.
Wants employer training schemes, not individual scrambling.

steps.text: Ask lecturers which software jobs still need humans
Apply to the university placement scheme for a year in industry
Try one AI coding tool for a month to see what it does

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster in the making and governments must step in now. Online I'd sign every petition for protection of workers. With my flatmates I'd be loud, probably too loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my degree becomes worthless before I finish it. Two years, and I'd be in my third year with a loan and a certificate for work a machine does cheaper. Robots for hands-on work come later, but that doesn't help someone who learned to code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to switch to something hands-on while there's still time, maybe an electrician apprenticeship, since robots are three years behind. I'd join the students' union campaign and go to every protest. And I'd stop spending anything I don't need, because the loan isn't going away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful. I'd be lying awake. Everything my mum worked for, the double shifts, would feel wasted, and I'd feel I let her down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is the warning time. What does that short warning do to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes away any plan. There's no time to retrain properly, no time for families to save. I'd run around in a panic, honestly, and the loan is still on my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to keep her shifts but stop sending money, and I'd say I'm going to look for a trade. She'd cry, and then she'd say fine, she always does.

say: I'd say governments must step in now and I'd sign every **petition** for worker protection.
I'd be loud with my flatmates, probably too loud.
think: My degree could be **worthless** before I finish, with the loan still on my back.
Two years gives no time to retrain or for families to save.
do: Look into an electrician **apprenticeship**, since robots reach hands-on work about three years later.
Join the students' union campaign and go to protests; cut every spending I can.
feel: I'd lie awake feeling I **let down** my mum after all her double shifts.
S2.quote: There's no time to retrain properly, no time for families to save. I'd run around in a panic, honestly, and the loan is still on my back.
fieldNote: Short warning removes his **sense of control**; he moves from steady worry to near panic.
Clear shift toward hands-on trades and collective action, in line with his politics.
Guilt about his mother's sacrifice is the emotional centre.

steps.text: Ask about electrician apprenticeships and switch courses if one opens
Join the students' union campaign and go to the protests
Stop all spending except rent and food
Sign petitions calling for worker protection laws

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives time to organise. I'd say we need a proper plan from the government, like retraining and support while jobs change. At the bike shop I'd say it's the same question, who gets the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate around 2030, right before the thinking AI arrives. That's scary, but at least I'd have a few years of study and maybe one placement before it hits. The hands-on world gets robots only around 2034, so a trade is still a decent escape hatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree but choose modules on hardware and electronics, not only pure coding. I'd do a placement in a small repair or engineering firm. And I'd start talking to the union about what help exists for graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but less panicked than the short one. Five years feels like seeing a storm on the horizon. You can still board up the windows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different with five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can finish the degree without throwing it away. With two years I'd bail out and start again, here I'd bend the plan. It still feels unfair though, that we have to do the bending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at your university would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who picked the course just for the money and never liked it. They have nothing to fall back on. My flatmate Kofi loves coding for its own sake, so he'd be fine whatever happens.

say: I'd say we need a government **plan** for retraining and support while jobs change.
At the bike shop I'd ask who actually gets the savings.
think: I'd graduate around 2030, just before **thinking AI** arrives, so time is tight.
Robots reach hands-on work around 2034, so a trade is still an escape route.
do: Pick **hardware** and electronics modules, not only pure coding.
Do a placement at a small engineering firm and ask the union what help exists.
feel: I feel **anxious** but calmer than with two years, like seeing a storm early.
S3.quote: Five years feels like seeing a storm on the horizon. You can still board up the windows.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **adjust** the plan instead of dropping it, which lowers his panic.
Worries most about classmates who chose the course only for money.
Politics drive his answer: he wants collective and public solutions.

steps.text: Choose hardware and electronics modules next year
Do a summer placement at a small engineering firm
Ask the students' union about help for graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot of time, so I'd say calm down and plan. I'd want governments to start retraining programmes early, and I'd back politicians who promise that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty by 2036 and I'd have time to try a couple of careers. It still bothers me that every plan I make might be wrong. But a decade is long enough to build savings, a trade skill and some contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take a first job, maybe in a small firm that does hardware and software together. In the first year I'd start learning a trade on the side, like basic electrics. And I'd try AI tools at last, slowly, since I'd have time to learn them properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. It's still a worry, but one I can plan around. I'd probably sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try AI tools finally. What changes your mind with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'm not being forced into it, so I can try it on my terms. If I'm panicked I refuse out of fear, but if I've got time I get curious. I'd still want a union or a lecturer to say what's safe to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from now if you knew it was ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop treating every module like an exam for survival. I'd take courses just because they're interesting, maybe philosophy, and not hurry. Honestly I'd probably worry less about my mum's money too.

say: I'd say stay calm and ask governments to start **retraining** programmes early.
I'd back politicians who promise real plans for graduates.
think: A **decade** is long enough to build savings, a trade skill and contacts.
I'm still afraid every plan I make might turn out wrong.
do: Finish the degree and take a first job at a small firm doing hardware and **software**.
Learn basic electrics on the side and try AI tools slowly, on my terms.
feel: I feel **better**, worried but able to plan around it.
S4.quote: If I'm panicked I refuse out of fear, but if I've got time I get curious.
fieldNote: The long warning turns his **fear** of AI tools into curiosity, which is a notable shift.
Still carries debt and money worry, so he doesn't drop all the way to calm.
Would like trusted guidance (union, lecturer) on what tools are safe.

steps.text: Take a first job at a small hardware and software firm
Learn basic electrics at an evening class
Try one AI tool slowly with a lecturer's advice

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fastest one, by far. Two years takes away the time to plan, and I'd have debt and a degree that nobody wants. What would help is the government acting early on retraining, a pause on loans for courses that vanish, and employers who train juniors instead of replacing them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as against technology as I sound. I just don't like being told what to think by companies that sell it. I'd like to understand it first and use it second.

headlineQuote: I'm not as against technology as I sound. I just don't like being told what to think by companies that sell it.
portrait: Diego is an **18-year-old** software engineering student; his nurse mum helps with rent and he works Saturdays at a bike shop.
He leans **progressive**, blames big companies and wants unions, rules and public retraining.
He is resistant to change, never uses AI tools, and would only try them reluctantly if the industry forced him.
His worry grows with speed: **uneasy** with no change, alarmed at two years, eased at ten.
Underneath everything is guilt about his mother's double shifts and the student loan.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, because it leaves no time to retrain and the loan stays.
whatWouldHelp: Early government **retraining**, employers who train juniors, and loan help for courses that lose their value.
